You control a blue circle that can move freely in a 2D white arena. A gray T-shaped block sits somewhere in the space. Your goal is to push that block until it perfectly overlaps with the green T-shaped goal drawn on the floor. The closer the block matches the goal in both position and orientation, the higher your reward.

You are a circular pusher operating in a flat, bounded arena. A T-shaped rigid block rests on the surface. A lighter green T-shape on the floor marks the target configuration. You must navigate around and into the block, using contact forces to slide and rotate it until it matches the target.

The environment contains four things: you (a blue circle), a movable gray T-block, a fixed green goal T, and static gray walls at the boundary. You can apply continuous velocity commands to move yourself. When you touch the T-block, you push it. Your task is complete when the T-block overlaps the green goal region.

The T-block starts at a random position and orientation each episode. The goal T is fixed and shown in green. You must plan a path that brings your body into contact with the appropriate face or corner of the T-block and then steer it — possibly re-approaching from multiple sides — until the block is seated on the goal.

The arena is enclosed by walls that prevent the block or yourself from leaving the play area. The T-block is rigid and cannot be directly grabbed — only pushed. Because you can only push (not pull), you may need to circle around the block multiple times to correct its angle before fully seating it on the green target.

You are a circular agent with continuous 2D velocity control. The environment is a white square arena enclosed by gray wall segments. Inside it, a gray T-shaped block sits at a random starting pose. The green T drawn on the floor is the goal — it shows you exactly where the block must end up, including its rotation angle. Your task is to contact the block and apply forces that drive it toward alignment with the goal. Because you can only push and not grip, steering the block's orientation requires careful choice of contact point and approach angle.

The T-block has an asymmetric shape: a wide horizontal bar on top and a narrower vertical stem below. This matters because to rotate the block clockwise you must push on its left side, and to rotate it counterclockwise you must push on its right side. Pushing straight through the block's center of mass translates it without rotating it. You must combine translation and rotation actions to match both the position and the angle of the green goal T.

At the start of each episode, the T-block is placed at a random position and orientation within the arena. The green goal T remains at a fixed location and orientation. You need to compute the relative transform between the current block pose and the goal pose, then plan a sequence of pushes that closes that gap. In general this requires: (1) rough translation push to bring the block near the goal XY position, (2) rotational pushes to align the block's heading with the goal heading, and (3) fine correction pushes to seat the block precisely on the goal.

Your reward signal is proportional to the area of overlap between the T-block footprint and the green goal T footprint. A score of 1.0 means perfect overlap. A score of 0.0 means no overlap. You should maximize cumulative overlap over the episode. Note that you can earn partial credit — even a partially aligned block scores better than no contact at all.

To push the block efficiently, approach it from behind relative to the direction you want the block to travel. Make contact and then drive forward, maintaining steady contact pressure. If the block drifts off course, disengage, reposition around the block, and re-approach from the corrected angle. The wall boundaries constrain the arena and will deflect both you and the block if contacted, so keep wall proximity in mind when planning maneuvers near the edges.

Because the T has rotational asymmetry (its stem extends only one way), the goal T and the block T can look similar from some angles but be 180 degrees misaligned. You must ensure that the stem of the block T points in the same direction as the stem of the goal T, not just that the shapes are co-located. A 180-degree rotation error produces partial overlap but not a perfect score.

To rotate the T-block, position yourself at an offset from its center of mass and push tangentially rather than radially. Pushing at the tip of the horizontal bar produces maximum torque and fastest rotation. Pushing near the center of the bar produces mostly translation. Use the corners and extremities of the T-shape as leverage points to spin the block efficiently.

The walls of the arena can be used strategically. If you need to rotate the block but cannot get a clean approach, you can pin the block against a wall and then push from the side, using the wall as a backstop to prevent the block from translating while you apply rotational force.

Your action space is a 2D continuous vector representing velocity commands in the X and Y axes of the arena. The arena has pixel-scale coordinates. You receive the current state as the XY position of the agent, the XY position of the T-block's center of mass, and the rotation angle of the T-block in radians. The goal is specified as a target XY position and target rotation angle that the T-block must reach. Minimize the L2 distance in position and the angular error in rotation between the current block pose and the goal pose simultaneously.

Contact between you and the T-block is simulated as rigid body pushing with no friction slip in the simulation's default configuration. When your circle overlaps the boundary of the T-shape, a contact normal force is applied to the block in the direction from your center toward the nearest block surface point. The magnitude of this force depends on the penetration depth. To maximize force transfer, approach perpendicular to the target face of the T-block at moderate speed — excessive speed causes the block to deflect unpredictably.

The full task decomposition is as follows. First, assess the current block pose relative to the goal pose. Compute the angular difference delta-theta and positional offset delta-X, delta-Y. Second, if delta-theta is large (more than ~30 degrees), prioritize rotation first: select a contact point on the block's periphery that maximizes torque about the block's center, then drive into that point from the appropriate side. Third, once orientation is roughly aligned, push the block's center of mass in the direction of the goal position. Fourth, make fine corrections by alternating between small rotational nudges and translational pushes. Finally, confirm alignment by checking that the block's stem points in the same direction as the goal stem.

The T-block has a distinctive geometry: the horizontal bar spans approximately three times the width of the stem, and the stem extends downward from the center of the bar. The block's center of mass sits near the junction of the bar and the stem. When you push directly through the center of mass, the block translates cleanly. When you push with lateral offset from the center of mass, you induce rotation. Larger offset produces more rotation per unit of force. Use this relationship to plan contact point selection.

Because you are a circle and the T-block is a polygon with both convex and concave edges (the inner corners where the stem meets the bar create concave regions), you will sometimes slip into the interior angles of the T-shape. When this happens you may become wedged. To escape, reverse away from the block, increase your lateral offset, and re-approach from a face that is convex and well-exposed. The outer corners and the three exposed faces of the bar, and the two side faces and bottom face of the stem, are all good contact surfaces.

At the start of each episode you must decide whether to: (a) push the block toward the goal position first and then rotate it once it is near, or (b) rotate the block toward the goal angle first and then translate it. Strategy (a) risks arriving at the goal position with the wrong orientation and then having difficulty rotating without drifting away. Strategy (b) risks accumulating translation error during the rotation phase. A hybrid approach — interleaved small rotations and translations — is generally most robust.

Reward shaping observation: the overlap metric is computed as the intersection area between the T-block polygon at its current pose and the goal T polygon at the fixed goal pose, divided by the total area of the T-shape. Intersection area is maximized when both position and angle match simultaneously, but partial position match with correct orientation scores reasonably well. Incorrect orientation with correct position scores poorly because the T-shapes' asymmetric stems create non-overlapping regions even when the bars are co-located.

An optimal policy for this task exhibits the following behavioral primitives: (1) approach primitive — move toward the block while computing the required contact angle; (2) contact primitive — make contact with the block at a predetermined point on its boundary; (3) push primitive — drive forward while maintaining contact and monitoring block displacement; (4) disengage primitive — reverse and reposition when the block trajectory diverges from the desired path; (5) align check — compare current block pose to goal pose and decide whether to continue pushing or reposition.

The task requires temporal credit assignment over long horizons. Early pushes that establish good block orientation pay off many steps later when translation to the goal is easier. A policy that optimizes only immediate reward may translate the block directly toward the goal without first correcting orientation, earning high short-term overlap but then struggling to make fine angular corrections near the goal, resulting in a local maximum below the perfect-score threshold.

Key failure modes to avoid: (a) pushing the block into a corner where it cannot be extracted, (b) repeatedly pushing the block past the goal because the agent does not decelerate before contact, (c) applying force through the block's center of mass when rotation is needed, (d) getting the orientation 180 degrees wrong due to the stem's symmetry ambiguity, (e) oscillating the block back and forth around the goal position without achieving stable alignment, (f) applying excessive force that causes the block to slide unpredictably off smooth floor contact.

When the angular error exceeds 90 degrees, a common efficient strategy is to push the block's top-right or top-left corner depending on the sign of the error. This creates high torque and spins the block quickly. Once the error is below 30 degrees, switch to pushing along the long axis of the block with a slight lateral offset to simultaneously close position and angle error. When error is below 10 degrees, approach very slowly and push near the center of mass almost directly in the direction of the remaining positional offset, accepting minimal rotational drift.

The success condition for this task is typically defined as: the intersection-over-union (IoU) between the T-block polygon and the goal T polygon exceeding a threshold, commonly 0.95. At this threshold the block must be within approximately 3–5 pixels of the target position and within approximately 5 degrees of the target angle in 512x512 pixel arena coordinates. Achieving this reliably requires sub-pixel-level precision in the final approach, which demands low-speed, high-accuracy final positioning moves.

For policy learning, note that this task has a highly multimodal action distribution at any given state. Given a block at a particular offset from the goal, there are at least two qualitatively different successful trajectories: go around the left side of the block and push right, or go around the right side and push left. Behavior cloning from a single demonstration mode will cause mode-averaging artifacts. Diffusion policy or other multimodal action distribution models are recommended to capture the full diversity of successful push trajectories.

Your observation at each timestep includes your own 2D position (a circle with radius R), the block's center of mass 2D position, and the block's current angle theta in [0, 2pi). The goal is specified by a fixed target position and target angle. The full relative state you should compute is: delta-x = block_x - goal_x, delta-y = block_y - goal_y, delta-theta = wrap_to_pi(block_theta - goal_theta), agent_x_relative_to_block, agent_y_relative_to_block. These five quantities fully characterize what action to take next given an optimal policy.

At reset, the block spawns at a uniformly random pose (x, y, theta) within the arena interior, with some minimum clearance from walls. The goal T is drawn at a fixed pose in the lower-center region of the arena. Episode length is 300 steps by default. Your average coverage over all 300 steps is the performance metric, meaning that you are rewarded even for transient overlap during the episode, not just for final-step alignment. This encourages the agent to get the block near the goal quickly and keep it there rather than spending most of the episode repositioning.

Imagine you are a hockey puck that can steer itself. On the ice in front of you is a T-shaped piece of wood. Your goal is to bump that piece of wood until it lands exactly on a green T-shaped outline painted on the ice. You cannot grab the wood — you can only push it. If you push too far to one side, the wood rotates. If you push straight through the middle, it slides. You have to figure out exactly which part of the wood to hit, and from which direction, to make it end up sitting perfectly on the painted outline.

Think of yourself as a robot arm that can only push, not grasp. The T-block is like an oddly shaped furniture piece you need to slide into a marked spot on the floor. Because it is T-shaped and not symmetric, you cannot simply push it from any side — you have to think about which pushes will rotate it and which will translate it, and sequence those pushes strategically to arrive at the target configuration.

The challenge of PushT is not finding the goal — the goal is right there, shown in green. The challenge is that every push simultaneously moves and rotates the block, and you cannot undo a push directly. You can only reposition yourself and push from the other side. This makes the task feel like a puzzle: each action changes the state in a coupled way, and solving it means learning to decouple translation and rotation through careful contact point selection.

The task feels easy at first — just push the block toward the green outline. But as the block gets close, you realize that the orientation is also wrong, and now correcting the angle without ruining the position is hard. Then you correct the angle but the position drifts. This iterative cycle of translation and rotation correction is the core motor skill this task trains. A good policy learns to plan both simultaneously rather than treating them sequentially.
Contact the T-block at a point and angle that produces the desired combination of translation and rotation.
You push; the block moves. Choose where to push so the movement brings the block closer to the green target.

Push slowly near the goal. Fast contact at close range overshoots and undoes your progress.
Use the walls as tools, not as obstacles, when you need a backstop for rotational pushes.
